gist: Indonesia is testing mosque loudspeakers to serve as earthquake early warning alarms.
A five-year joint research trial with Japanese scientists aims to reach remote communities.
Researchers are tailoring survival strategies to Indonesia's vulnerable, low-rise masonry buildings.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Scientists in earthquake-prone Indonesia have launched a pilot scheme linking mosque loudspeakers to a seismic sensor network. Conceived by Japanese disaster scientist Dr Inoue Hiroshi, the five-year project assesses whether speakers used for prayer calls can double as earthquake warning klaxons. Several mosques have already been hooked up to the system.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques with well-maintained loudspeakers reaching remote areas where mobile infrastructure may fail during earthquakes. Because seismic waves travel rapidly, nearby communities might have only five to ten seconds to react. Additionally, unreinforced buildings in Indonesia mean international advice like "drop and cover" is often unsuitable, prompting tailored survival guidance.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Running until 2030, the prototype initiative aims to eventually issue public alerts. Researchers plan to test alarms via school loudspeakers, radio, and television, whilst conducting simulations and human experiments to develop science-based survival guidelines.
